hints: Start at the top of Fig. 5.1 and trace the path air takes inward - what is the large tube with rings, and what does it split into to enter each lung?
Think about how tubes get smaller and more numerous inside the lung to increase surface area - what are the names of the progressively smaller airways?
Finish the journey where gas exchange actually happens - what are the tiny air sacs called, and which large paired organs contain them all?
walkthrough:
Follow the Airway From Outside to Inside**
You can see the trachea at the top of Fig. 5.1 with its C-shaped cartilage rings that hold it open. It branches into two main bronchi, one supplying each lung. That branching is the key gross feature - one tube becoming two.

Branching Inside the Lung**
Inside the lung each bronchus keeps dividing into smaller tubes called bronchioles. This repeated branching creates a tree-like network that carries air deep into all regions of the lung.

The Exchange Surface**
The smallest bronchioles end in clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli. The two lungs contain millions of alveoli, giving a huge surface for gas exchange. So a full answer names trachea, bronchus, bronchiole, alveoli and lungs in correct sequence.
Final answer: Trachea divides into two bronchi, one to each lung; bronchi branch into smaller bronchioles; bronchioles end in alveoli where gas exchange occurs.

hints: Recall what nicotine does while smoking - it stimulates the nervous system and constricts blood vessels, so what must reverse when it is gone?
Link constricted vessels and stimulation to two easy measurements a doctor takes at the wrist and with a cuff - what happens to those values?
walkthrough:
Remember What Nicotine Was Doing**
Nicotine causes vasoconstriction, meaning smooth muscle in arteriole walls contracts and the lumen narrows. It also stimulates increased heart rate and makes platelets more sticky. It also raises blood pressure.

Reverse the Effects**
When nicotine falls, vessels relax so lumen diameter increases and blood pressure decreases back toward normal. Heart rate also decreases back toward normal. Platelets are less likely to stick, so risk of blood clot and damage to endothelium leading to atheroma is reduced. Any two of these changes gain credit.
Final answer: Blood pressure decreases to normal; heart rate decreases to normal; less vasoconstriction / wider vessel lumen; platelets less sticky so lower risk of thrombosis.

hints: Compare the tops of curves A and B at high $pO_2$ around $10-14$ $kPa$ - what is the maximum percentage saturation for the smoker versus after stopping?
Think about why curve A can never reach 100% - which gas in smoke binds irreversibly to haemoglobin and blocks oxygen?
Look at the steep middle part and the tissue end at low $pO_2$ - how does a normal curve allow more oxygen to be picked up in lungs and released in respiring tissues?
Link more oxygen delivery to what cells can now do better - why does this mean less fatigue and better exercise ability?
walkthrough:
Describe What the Graph Shows**
In the lungs $pO_2$ is high, on the right side of Fig. 5.2. Curve A for the heavy smoker plateaus at only about 79% saturation, while curve B after stopping reaches about 98%. For example at $8$ $kPa$, saturation rises from about 75% to about 88%. That is a large increase in oxygen carried.

Explain the Carbon Monoxide Effect**
Carbon monoxide has a much higher affinity for haemoglobin than oxygen and forms carboxyhaemoglobin. While smoking, many of the four haem groups on each haemoglobin are permanently blocked. After stopping, no more CO binds, so more sites are free to bind oxygen in the lungs.

Loading and Unloading Benefit**
With free sites, haemoglobin becomes more saturated in the lungs at high $pO_2$. In respiring tissues where $pO_2$ is low, that extra oxyhaemoglobin can dissociate to release more oxygen. Curve B regains its normal sigmoid shape and normal allosteric loading and unloading.

Link to Health**
More oxygen is transported and delivered to respiring tissues for aerobic respiration. The person feels less tired and can do more work or exercise. Always quote both curves with values in $kPa$ and % to support the description, then give the CO explanation.

Final answer: After stopping, saturation at high $pO_2$ rises from approx 79% (curve A) to approx 98% (curve B), e.g. at $8$ $kPa$ approx 75% to approx 88%; CO no longer forms carboxyhaemoglobin so more haem sites free for $O_2$; more $O_2$ loaded in lungs and unloaded at respiring tissues, improving aerobic respiration and activity.

hints: Think about what the word infectious means - what type of agent must be involved and able to spread between people?
Contrast that with lung cancer - what starts it inside the lung, from tar carcinogens rather than from another person?
walkthrough:
What Infectious Means**
An infectious disease is caused by a pathogen such as a bacterium or virus that can be transmitted from an infected person to another person.

Why Lung Cancer Is Different**
Lung cancer is uncontrolled division of the person's own lung cells, triggered by carcinogens in tar, not by a pathogen. It cannot spread by infection from one person to another, so it is classed as non-infectious even though it is a disease - an abnormal condition affecting the body.
Final answer: Not caused by a pathogen / transmissible agent; cannot be passed from person to person; is abnormal uncontrolled cell division / abnormal condition of the body.
